meta.title: The River Keeps Its Name
meta.theme: why place names outlive the languages that coined them

format.format_verified: 2026-09: recent CAT papers set Para Summary among the non-negative verbal questions; re-verify against each new official paper

apex.claim: Names tend to survive a change of language better than ordinary words do, because a name is learned as a label rather than understood as a word and so passes on untranslated; but this is a tendency, and names can still be swept away.
apex.scope: River and hill names in regions that have undergone language shift, stated as a tendency with an explicit exception where settlers arrive in numbers.

meta.learning_objective: keep the limit an author attaches to a tendency, when the mechanism behind it sounds strong enough to be a rule

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival is the option that concedes the fate of ordinary vocabulary and then promises a name will survive any change of language. It reproduces the paragraph's contrast and its mechanism exactly, and the last clause removes it: the survival is 'not reliable', settlers who arrive in numbers rename freely, and a name can be lost in a single generation. The option reporting names being older than the languages spoken there is the observation with the explanation stripped out, and the option about anything learned as a whole outlasting what is understood carries a claim about names to every kind of unanalysed material.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement; options rewritten 2026-09-13 to remove the shape tells (a genuine concessive clause now sits in a distractor); awaits re-solve; x

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General reasoning about toponymic survival across language shift; no specific region or text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: A clean mechanism with an explicit limit in the last clause. Three distortion families: certainty (the tendency hardened), structure (the observation without the explanation), scope (names widened to everything learned unanalysed).

sentences.text: In many regions the names of the rivers and the hills are older than any language now spoken there.
A name is learned as a label rather than as a word with parts, so a newcomer can take it over without knowing, or needing to know, what it once meant.
Ordinary vocabulary has no such protection: it is understood, and what is understood can be translated and replaced.
Names therefore tend to survive a change of language better than words do, though not reliably: settlers who arrive in numbers rename freely, and a name can be lost in a single generation.

ideal_summary: Names tend to outlast a change of language better than ordinary words, because they are taken over as labels rather than understood and translated, though they can still be lost.

builder.prompt: In one sentence: why do names outlast languages, according to the paragraph, and how far does the claim go?

checks.ask: Does your sentence give the reason names survive, rather than only reporting that they do?
checks.kept: Good. The reason is the whole argument: a label can be handed on without being understood, and what is understood is what gets translated.
checks.drifted: That old names outlast languages is the observation the paragraph opens with. The claim is the mechanism that explains it.

checks.ask: Did you keep 'tend to' and the acknowledgement that names are sometimes lost?
checks.kept: Exactly. The final clause is there to stop a good mechanism from becoming a law, and the summary has to carry it.
checks.drifted: 'Any change of language' is stronger than the text. The paragraph says settlers arriving in numbers rename freely and a name can go in a single generation.

checks.ask: Is your sentence about names, or about everything that is learned without being understood?
checks.kept: Well held. The comparison the paragraph draws is between names and ordinary vocabulary, and its evidence is entirely about places.
checks.drifted: Formulae, songs and habits are never discussed here. A claim about all unanalysed material rests on arguments the paragraph has not made.

question.stem: Which option best captures the essence of the paragraph?

options.A: Although ordinary words get translated and replaced, a place name will survive any change of language at all, since no one need know what it means to use it.
options.B: In a great many regions the names given to the rivers and the hills turn out to be a good deal older than any of the languages that are spoken there today.
options.C: Anything at all that is learned as a whole rather than understood will outlast what is understood, wherever one language gradually gives way to another.
options.D: Names tend to outlive a change of language because they are learned as labels, not understood, though settlers arriving in numbers can sweep them away.

explanation.paragraph_meaning: Rivers and hills in many places carry names that are older than any language now heard there. The reason is that a name is not really a word to the people who inherit it. It is a label, and you can use a label perfectly well without knowing what it once described, so it passes from one population to the next untouched. Ordinary words are different: people know what they mean, and anything understood can be translated and swapped for a local equivalent. So names travel through a change of language better than vocabulary does. Not always, though. Where settlers arrive in force they rename as they please, and an old name can disappear inside one generation.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries the mechanism, that a name is taken over as a label rather than understood, and keeps the limit the last clause sets, that names can still be swept away. It reports a tendency, which is the author's own word.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph does contrast names with ordinary vocabulary, so the concession is its own; what follows is not. It says names survive better but 'not reliably', and names the exception: settlers who arrive in numbers rename freely, and a name can be lost in a single generation.
distractors.seductive_element: It borrows the paragraph's comparison and its mechanism, so the only thing added is the word that turns a tendency into a rule, and that word is easy to read past.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Letting a convincing explanation license a stronger claim than the author was prepared to make.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the opening observation, which the rest of the paragraph exists to explain. Nothing of the explanation, and nothing of the comparison with ordinary vocabulary, appears here.
distractors.seductive_element: It is a striking fact and it cannot be wrong, since it is lifted from the first sentence.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Summarising the phenomenon a paragraph sets out to account for rather than the account it gives.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph compares names with ordinary vocabulary, and every piece of evidence in it concerns places. Extending the claim to all unanalysed material covers cases the argument has not examined.
distractors.seductive_element: It states the general principle the names appear to instance, and general principles look like the deeper summary.
distractors.thinking_mistake: Abstracting away from the category an author argued about, on the assumption that a wider claim is a better one.

explanation.reading_habit: Read past the colon in a final sentence. Authors often put a mechanism before it and the exception after it, and only the exception decides between the options.

mentor.challenge: The explanation here is good enough to sound like a law. The last clause of the paragraph says it is not one.
mentor.takeaway: A word survives by not being understood. That is a tendency, not a guarantee.
